decisions.question: e-6854

source.question: e-6854
source.value:
The volume of the cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3} \pi r^2h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(r,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi rh\,\text{d}r+\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=6$ and $h=3,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,3) & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot 6\cdot 3\,\text{d}r+\frac{1}{3}\pi \cdot {6}^{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =12\pi \,\text{d}r+12\pi \,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

source.value: If $f (x, y) = xe^y ,$ use the differential $\textrm d f$ to estimate the change $\Delta f$ in the value of $f(x, y)$ from $(5,0)$ to $(2,1).$

decisions.reason: Observed MA content supersedes the stored value

decisions.question: e-6875

source.question: e-6875
source.value:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={e}^{y}\,\text{d}x+x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(5,0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(5,0) & ={e}^{0}\,\text{d}x+5{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+5\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(5 + \Delta x, 0 + \Delta y),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
\Delta f \approx 1 \, \Delta x + 5 \, \Delta y.
$$

Moving from $(5,0)$ to $(2,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =2-5=-3, \\ Δy & =1-0=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+5\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-3)+5\cdot (1) \\  & ≈2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $2.$

decisions.question: e-6876

source.question: e-6876
source.value:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $\left( \pi, 0 \right),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,\text{d}y \\  & =-1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(\pi + \Delta x, 0 + \Delta y),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
\Delta f \approx  -1  \,  \Delta x + 0  \,  \Delta y
$$

Note that 

$$
\sin (3) + \cos (0.2)= f(3,0.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3,0.2).$

Moving from $(\pi, 0)$ to $(3,0.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3-\pi ≈-0.141, \\ Δy & =0.2-0=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈-1(-0.141)+0(0.2) \\  & ≈0.141.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.141.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,0.2) & ≈f(\pi ,0)+0.141 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0.2) & ≈\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+0.141 \\  & ≈0+1+0.141 \\  & ≈1.141.\end{aligned}
$$
